title: LUMLON
pitch: Is the air safe today? LUMLON answers for a person and for an agent through the same six site tools — and tells the agent when its own hazard data has expired.
about_excerpt: Is the air safe today? LUMLON answers for a person and for an agent through the same six site tools — and tells the agent when its own hazard data has expired. Like Comment Story Updates The page reads three provinces on load and plots all 77. Every card carries its observation time and source — before any agent arrives. Six site tools, declared by the page itself — no plugin, no separate server. Watches live in this browser only, never on a server. Asked about official warnings, the agent reads the expiry itself and refuses to report an expired warning as current. Nobody told it to. Inspiration Every morning I check the same thing: what is the air like today, is it safe, and can I play tennis with my son this evening? I check because my son was admitted to the hospital for it: a severe asthma attack, his airways closing, after breathing PM2.5 over a stretch of days when readings in our area were many times the level the World Health Organization calls safe. That is why "is the air safe today?" is not a curiosity in my house. It is a decision, every morning, before anything else gets decided. So I started building LUMLON: a Thai app that reads air, weather, and hazard conditions in real time. It exists, and you can open it — https://lumlon-web-dev.vercel.app is our development build, mid-redesign and not launched yet. I would rather you looked than took my word for it. What it is for is simple — to tell a person, day by day, at a time they choose or the moment they ask, whether it is safe to be outside. Not so they can study a chart, but so a father and son can plan an ordinary evening without gambling on it. Air you can plan around is also cheaper than a hospital admission, and in my family, that is not a figure of speech. The data already exists. Checking it does not scale. Today that means jumping between several apps, government agencies, and websites — each with its own shape, its own gaps, and its own idea of what "no data" means. It takes time, and on a morning you are in a hurry, you skip it. Would it not be better to simply ask — or to be told at the moments that matter — without opening anything at all? That is the kind of problem WebMCP is actually for. The person asking does not want a dashboard; they want an answer, in their own words, about their own province, right now. And people have already moved. They reach for an AI tool first now, which makes an agent a practical way to get this kind of information to someone — not a novelty. LUMLON was always meant to reach people through whatever channel they already use, not only inside one app. What WebMCP adds is that the answer can come from us: specific readings, each carrying its source and the time it was taken, instead of whatever an agent can assemble on its own. An agent also does something a website cannot do for everyone at once — it turns a reading into an answer in the language and the words of whoever is asking. That is why one of these six tools does not return a number at all. It returns a judgment about a specific activity, together with the readings it used and the reason it reached that answer. A number tells you what the air is like. A person still has to decide whether to go outside. So we did not build a chatbot on top of a website. We made the website itself something an agent can read, and kept the human looking at the same screen the whole time. What it does LUMLON exposes six tools to any WebMCP-capable agent, for all 77 provinces of Thailand. Tool What it does Kind search_locations Turns a place name into a province code. Thai or English, loose spelling. read get_environment_snapshot Air quality, short forecast, and official hazard alerts — each alert carries its own expiry, because they come from a dated snapshot. read get_safety_briefing Decides whether an activity is advisable and explains why , quoting the readings. read create_watch Saves a rule that warns when a reading crosses a threshold. write list_watches Lists the rules saved in this browser. read delete_watch Removes one rule. destructive It is a working page before an agent arrives. Open it with no agent at all and it reads three provinces on load — live PM2.5 and AQI, plus the official hazard alerts from a dated snapshot, which every card says on its face — and plots them on a map of all 77 provinces drawn from our own registry. You can search a province in Thai or English and read it yourself, with one click, through the same data path a tool call takes. This matters for a reason beyond looks: an agent-ready site can only be judged on what the agent adds , and that needs a "before" to compare against. A blank page waiting for a tool call is not a product an agent improves — it is a log viewer. What people and agents do together, concretely. You ask "is the air safe for a morning run in Chiang Mai tomorrow?" The agent calls two tools and answers in a sentence. At the same moment, the page in front of you updates — the same reading, the same timestamp, the same source. The map moves to Chiang Mai on its own; the card that appears is labelled read by the agent , next to cards labelled read by this page , so you can always tell which of the two of you did what. You did not lose the screen by talking to an agent; you gained a second way to drive it. Then you say "watch this and warn me if it goes above 75," and a rule appears as a card you can see — and that you remove the same way you made it, by asking. The panel lists your watches; it does not hide them, and it does not let anything but a tool call change them. The map moves without a seventh tool. We deliberately did not add a set_map_view tool to let the agent pan the screen. The view follows the tools it already has: search a place, the camera frames it; read a place, the pin lights up. Tool descriptions are charged against the agent's context on every single turn, so a tool is a cost, not an achievement — and this one would have bought nothing that the existing events did not already carry. Three decisions that make this usable rather than merely present: Every block of data carries when it was observed and where it came from. A number without a timestamp is a number nobody can check — and the person hearing an agent read it aloud cannot see the screen to judge for themselves. Missing data is reported, never hidden. If a source cannot be read, the answer says so, in a gaps field the agent reads out. "Could not read" and "there are no alerts" are different facts, and collapsing them is the single most dangerous thing a safety tool can do. For the same reason, a briefing never says good while something it needed was unavailable: missing data can lower our confidence, but it never lowers a warning. Read tools and write tools fail in opposite directions, on purpose. A read tool with one number missing still answers the question that was actually asked, and names what it could not read. A write tool with anything unvalidated refuses the whole command. Both write tools are annotated as writes, and delete_watch is additionally marked destructive. In the session we recorded — with approvals set to allow everything — the agent still stopped and asked before it deleted a rule. How we built it The tools do not know where their data comes from. They only ever talk to a provider interface, and that interface is in this repository: src/webmcp/providers/types.ts . The implementation behind it here is the bundled one, which calls only public sources. Be precise about what you can and cannot check in this export. The second implementation — the one that reads the backend of the product we are building — is not in this repository. The export is generated by following what the shipped entry actually imports, and since this entry runs on the bundled provider, the other implementation is never reached and never copied. So what you can verify here is the seam, not both sides of it: one interface, one implementation, and six tool files that name neither. That seam is the reason this entry can be frozen for judging while the product keeps moving, and it is also the reason we are telling you the second half is missing instead of letting the sentence imply it is here. To be exact about what that does and does not mean: this WebMCP layer was built for this challenge, and the product ships with it switched off. The shared interface is what makes it portable — not a claim that agents are driving our production app today. The module is invisible when it is off. WebMCP registration lives behind a build flag and a dynamic import. With the flag off, a scan of our own build output finds no trace of the module — 2,838 files swept, zero hits, on the tree we build from. We check this rather than asserting it, because we found the opposite of what we assumed the first time we measured: an unset environment variable is not a constant, so the bundler could not prove the branch was dead, and it emitted the chunk anyway.
